specAnchors.text: understand that a disproportionation reaction involves an element in a single species being simultaneously oxidised and reduced

primer.text: Some reactions split one species against itself: a single element is pushed up and down the oxidation ladder at the same time. That double life is disproportionation. This note defines it, walks the chlorine-in-alkali case ion by ion, and shows the five-step balancing routine that turns observation into a tidy equation.

modules.title: One element, two directions
modules.opening: Disproportionation is a split personality reaction: a single element inside one species simultaneously climbs and falls on the oxidation ladder. This lesson defines the phenomenon and shows the chlorine-in-water case where one chlorine atom oxidises another from the same starting molecule.
keyPoints: A disproportionation reaction involves one species being simultaneously oxidised and reduced.
The same element divides into two products at different oxidation numbers.
In chlorine water, Cl2 splits into chloride at -1 and chlorate(I) at +1.
The starting element sits at 0, exactly between the two destinations.
Both a reduction leg and an oxidation leg run inside one reaction.

low.restatement: One species starts at one oxidation number and ends split across two - one leg up, one leg down - which is why the reaction is named dis-proportion-ation: the proportions divide.
low.analogy: One ladder, two climbers: the same person's identical twins start on the same rung, and one steps up while the other steps down at the same instant.
low.examPointer: Quote both destination states with signs when identifying disproportionation - one up and one down from the same start is the whole signature.

medium.restatement: The element's initial state must sit between its two product states; the electron ledger closes internally because the electrons lost on the oxidation leg are exactly those gained on the reduction leg, with no outside partner needed.
medium.analogy: A self-contained transaction: the same account splits its balance, transferring internally so the books balance without any external counterparty.
medium.examPointer: If asked why a species cannot disproportionate, show it lacks an accessible state on both sides of its current one.

modules.title: Balancing chlorine in hot alkali, step by step
modules.opening: The five-step routine turns observation into a balanced equation. This lesson walks chlorine through hot concentrated sodium hydroxide to chloride and chlorate(V), watching the oxidation numbers drive every coefficient.
keyPoints: Step 1 writes the unbalanced equation and flags the atoms that change oxidation number.
Step 2 deduces the changes: chlorine falls 0 to -1 and climbs 0 to +5.
Step 3 balances the ledger: one atom up 5 needs five atoms down 1.
Step 4 balances charge with hydroxide ions, and step 5 balances atoms with water.

low.restatement: Write the skeleton, read the state changes off chlorine, scale so the up-leg equals the down-leg, patch charge with hydroxide, then patch atoms with water until everything closes.
low.analogy: Repairing a see-saw: first spot which rider moved (states), then add counterweights (coefficients) until both sides level out (balance).
low.examPointer: Never skip step 2 - writing the 0 to -1 and 0 to +5 changes explicitly is where the method marks live.

medium.restatement: The 5-unit climb per chlorine to chlorate(V) demands five 1-unit falls to chloride, fixing the 5Cl- to 1ClO3- ratio; six hydroxides then deliver six negative charges matching the six product ions, and three waters absorb the leftover hydrogens and oxygens.
medium.analogy: A payroll where one manager draws a 5-unit bonus paid by five staff at 1 unit each - the coefficients are the headcount the ledger forces.
medium.examPointer: Check the final equation by atom census: 6 Cl, 6 O and 6 H appear on each side - a failed census means a wrong coefficient upstream.

glossary.definition: A reaction in which one species is simultaneously oxidised and reduced, splitting one element across two product states.
The ClO3- ion, where chlorine sits at oxidation number +5 and forms in hot concentrated alkali.
The electron bookkeeping that balances every unit climbed against every unit fallen in a redox equation.

workedExample.prompt: Balance the disproportionation of chlorine in hot concentrated aqueous sodium hydroxide, where the products are Cl-, ClO3- and water.
steps: Step 1 - write the skeleton: Cl2 -> Cl- + ClO3- and flag chlorine as the changing atom.
Step 2 - deduce the changes: chlorine falls from 0 to -1 and climbs from 0 to +5.
Step 3 - balance the ledger: one atom climbing 5 units needs five atoms falling 1 unit, so 5Cl- per ClO3-.
Step 4 - balance charge: 6OH- on the left matches the 6 negative charges among 5Cl- and ClO3-.
Step 5 - balance atoms: 3H2O absorbs the 6 hydrogens and 3 extra oxygens, giving 3Cl2 + 6OH- -> 5Cl- + ClO3- + 3H2O.
workedExample.finalAnswer: 3Cl2 + 6OH- -> 5Cl- + ClO3- + 3H2O, with chlorine split 5 down to -1 and 1 up to +5.
